full_judgment: 5. The respondent No. 1 has filed an application for vacating the interim injunction on 12-6-2012, pursuant to an application filed on 22-7-2012 by the Respondent No.1. which was later on converted to affidavit-in-opposition. The main contention of the respondent No. 1 is that, the respondent No. 1 has suffered loss of almost US $ 4 million due to the of the petitioner, the amount guaranteed by the Bank-Guarantee No.411020019910 dated 31-1-2010 only represents a fraction of the same, and based on the assessment of performance of the, petitioner there would be a resolution of the final amount; that the subject matter of the contract is the performance by the petitioner and that the Bank-Guarantee is not the subject matter of the contract or of any arbitration arising out of the contract. The Bank-Guarantee by its very nature was for immediate encashment and if there is any grievance of the petitioner regarding the amount paid or received, that would be a money claim and can be satisfied with a money decree one way or another and there would be no prospect of the petitioner being prejudiced. On the other hand, if encashment of a bank-guarantee, which by its very nature has to be cashed upon demand, is made subject to arbitration proceedings, the very reason and purpose of the bank-guarantee would be vitiated. Thus a bank-guarantee cannot be subject matter of a "protective order" under section 7Ka of the. Arbitration Act 2001; that encasement of the Bank-Guarantee will not in any manner prejudice the arbitration proceedings nor shall it make the arbitration proceedings or any award passed by the tribunal, even in favour, of the petitioner, in fructuous. The nature of claim and award would be monetary in nature, hence, does not merit interference at this stage; that an application under section 7A of the Arbitration Act 2001 can only be filed before the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh if the arbitration is an International Commercial Arbitration within the meaning of section 2(c) of the Arbitration Act 2001. Since the petitioner does not fall within the purview of section 2(c) of the Arbitration Act 2001, the instant dispute between the petitioner and the respondents does not qualify to mandate an International Commercial Arbitration; that the Petitioner and respondent No. 1 are companies incorporated in Bangladesh and thus this is not an international arbitration. The petitioner claims to fall within the ambit of section 2(c)(3) of the Arbitration Act 2001. However, in order to fall within the ambit of section 2(c)(3) of the Arbitration Act 2001, both the management and the control of the company must be exercised in a place outside Bangladesh. The petitioner does not satisfy this criterion since the place where its management and control is exercised is not outside Bangladesh and, as such, in not covered by section 2(c) (3) of the Arbitration Act 2001; that although the petitioner is admittedly a subsidiary of Siemens GmbH, that does not have any bearing over the place where management and control of the petitioner is exercised. According to section 2(4) of the Companies Act. 1994, whether a company is a subsidiary of another is determined by the shareholding position of that company and not by where its management and control is exercised. Even if the entire shareholding of a subsidiary company is totally owned by its parent company, it is perfectly possible for the same to exercise its management and power inside Bangladesh and not from outside. The criteria under section 2(c) (3) of the Arbitration Act 2001 is not based on shareholding, but on the "place of exercise" of central and management; that under Article 126 of the Articles of Association of the petitioner company the Managing Director of the petitioner is capable of being empowered to make key management decisions and sign essential contracts on behalf of the company is based in Bangladesh upon passing a Board resolution to that effect. The directors of the petitioner company are based in Bangladesh, India and Germany. However, all Board Meetings, EGM and AGM of the petitioner Company take place in Bangladesh. The registered address and office of the petitioner company is in Bangladesh. Moreover, the petitioner company executes commercial contracts with its parent company in the capacity 'of a separate legal entity, which can only mean that the Bangladesh entity has a separate management and control which is exercised in its place of business, being Bangladesh. Hence, this petition is not maintainable before this court.
